content.text:
Claudinite loaded, 9 packs, 41 checks, 16,500 rule tokens, 19 available skills, 9 personal preference rules.

Let me take the three claims in order, because I want to concede two of them partially and push back on where the correctness weight actually sits.

## "No atomic check-and-apply on labels" — true, but the design never asks labels to deconflict

You're right that GitHub has no label CAS, and if the protocol were "check label, apply label, trust the label," it would be broken. But the design explicitly routes around that: **labels are visibility and pick filters, never the arbiter** (§6.2, and the sim README's "Label API atomicity" row says exactly this). The arbiter is the claim *comment*, and comment creation **is** an atomic primitive with a server-assigned total order: every executor posts its claim, re-reads, and the lowest comment id wins. Two executors both passing the label check and both swapping labels is an anticipated, harmless outcome — the torn label state is repaired (janitor's stateless-item rule), and ownership was never derived from it.

So the honest question is whether the *comment* lease is sound without CAS — and the design names its one residual assumption itself (sim README, "Claim-comment interleaving"): *a comment list read after posting includes all earlier-id comments*. If GitHub's read-after-write on comment lists is ever weaker than that, two claimants can each see themselves as earliest. That's the real soft spot, not labels — and note that jitter and randomization don't fix it either; they only make it rarer. The design already records the actual fix for that contingency: **§15.10, ref-creation CAS** — `refs/claudinite/claim/<n>` is GitHub's one true first-writer-wins primitive, recorded as the drop-in replacement for the comment lease "unless a real lost-race incident occurs." So if your concern is "the deconfliction primitive is shaky," the right escalation on the books is deterministic (ref CAS), not probabilistic (spreading).

## The 4-second jitter — conceded, with the mechanism named

You're right that it doesn't ruin predictability — it sits before the claim, changes no outcome, and only spreads arrivals. And on reflection it helps more than I credited last turn, in the *common* collision case: the drain run and an event-fired run going for the same single item. Jitter gives the first claimant's `task:ready → task:executing` swap time to land and propagate, so the second executor's pick filter sees `task:executing` and **skips cleanly instead of entering the claim race at all** — the conflict resolves at the cheap filter layer rather than the comment-arbitration layer. That's a genuine reduction in protocol exercise, not just probability-shaving. Cost: ~4s added latency on event-fired pickups, nothing on correctness, one line in the executor. I'd call it a reasonable amendment; the sim doesn't need to model it (it changes race frequency, not race outcome, and races stay explicitly constructed via `raceExecutorsAt`).

## Randomized pick order — the one I'd still push back on, for a scale reason

Randomization lowers collision probability only when there are **multiple ready items to spread over**. Its win is ~1/k collision probability across a queue of depth k — but this system's steady-state queue depth is approximately **one**: the standing-item model means quiet tasks sit blocked, and a drain typically finds zero or one ready item (S1′/S22). In the dominant collision case — two executors and the single item an event just announced — randomization has nothing to shuffle and does exactly nothing; jitter is the measure that helps there. Randomization starts paying off in the regime the design doesn't inhabit: deep queues and many executors (the late-fire catch-up morning is the only deep-queue moment, and there the items are mostly chain-ordered by the `after` yield anyway).

Against that marginal win, the cost is small but real: oldest-first is what bounds an item's wait and keeps the janitor's stale-ready escalation (~2 periods, keyed on ready-age) meaning "something is wrong" rather than "unlucky shuffles." At depth ~1 that cost is also ~0 — which is my point in both directions: **at this scale, randomizing and not randomizing are nearly indistinguishable**, so I'd keep the deterministic order for its testability and fairness semantics, and let jitter carry the contention reduction. If executor count ever grows to where pick collisions are measured (the migration burst's B-rows is where that would show), randomized-after-urgent is the cheap first knob and I'd have no objection then.

**Summary position**: correctness rests on the comment lease (and its named escalation path, ref CAS §15.10) — neither proposal touches that layer. Jitter: worth adopting, for the filter-layer-resolution reason above. Randomization: near-zero effect at queue depth ~1; defer until contention is observed.

> ✅ Analysis delivered, nothing changed. Still open: whether to amend DESIGN.md — (a) add the ~4s claim jitter to §6.1, (b) adopt randomized pick order now vs. defer, (c) optionally note the comment-list read-after-write assumption's escalation path more prominently. Say the word and I'll fold any of these into the design.

content.text:
Claudinite loaded, 9 packs, 41 checks, 16,500 rule tokens, 19 available skills, 9 personal preference rules.

Direct answers to the three questions, and then the part you're dreading — which is half true, but less alarming than it sounds.

## How does a tick-readied item get picked up immediately?

Structurally, not by event: **the executor is a job in the same workflow run as the tick** (§10 — "the tick runs first; the executor drains what it created, which keeps the common case's latency at zero even without events"). The tick's job 1/2 create and ready items; the drain job in that same run then lists `task:ready` and works through them. No label event is needed, so the `GITHUB_TOKEN` suppression costs nothing on this path — the design's "sub-minute pickup" for scheduled work never depended on events firing.

The `labeled` event trigger matters only for items readied by a **foreign token between ticks**: a human forcing/waking an item, `create-work-item` on a PAT, a CCR agent fanning out items. Those writes do fire events (they're not `GITHUB_TOKEN`), and that's exactly the urgent-work path S16 tests. So the two trigger paths partition cleanly: own-token writes are drained in-run; foreign-token writes get real events; and anything that falls through both is caught by the next tick's drain — "events are latency sugar, the poll is the guarantee."

## After an executor finishes an item, what picks up the next one?

Nothing *fires* — **the same run loops**: §6's "An executor run may iterate (claim → … → hand off, next pick) up to a configured `maxItems`." When the run exits (queue drained, or `maxItems` hit, or timeout), leftover ready items simply wait for the next trigger: the next tick's drain (≤1h) or the next foreign-token event. Same for items that become ready *because* of a finished item: a dependent's `Blocked-by` flips only at the tick (§15.8 — "dependency readiness is the tick's alone"), so chain links are tick-quantized at ~1h each. That's F1, raised in the scenarios and **declined by you on 2026-08-13** ("~1h/link is within tolerance") — worth re-checking that call now that you're looking at it from this angle.

## And yes — one executor run iterates all the ready items. Here's why that's not what it sounds like

The dread reading is "one run serially does a whole night's work." What actually serializes is thin: per item, the executor does **claim → precondition → prework → async API hand-off** and moves on. The agentic work — the expensive part — runs in **parallel CCR sessions**, one per handed-off item; the executor never waits for an agent. So on the late-fire morning with five items, one drain run hands off five sessions in a few minutes and they all run concurrently.

The genuine serial cost is **prework**, which runs inline in the executor (minutes each, and baselining's converge is the heavy one). A run's budget is bounded twice — `maxItems` and `timeout-minutes ≤ the 1h executing leash` — so one run *can't* balloon; it drains what fits and leaves the rest for the next trigger. When that's not enough, the design's scaling answers (§10) are: raise `maxItems`, run **parallel executor jobs as a matrix width**, or add executors outside Actions — each item is independently leased, so width is safe by construction. What the design does *not* have is self-chaining ("executor finishes, fires the next executor"). If you ever want sub-tick chaining, the platform's sanctioned loophole exists: `workflow_dispatch` is one of the two events a `GITHUB_TOKEN` *can* trigger, so a drain that exits with ready items left (or a converge that closes a blocker) could re-dispatch the executor workflow. That would pair naturally with reopening F1's converger-poke — but both are currently declined/absent, and at today's queue depths (~0–1 ready items outside catch-up mornings) the tick cadence genuinely covers it.

> ✅ Analysis only, nothing changed. Still open, if the ~1h quantization now bothers you: (a) reopen F1 (converger pokes readiness in code) and/or (b) add self-re-dispatch via `workflow_dispatch` for drains that exit with items remaining — both are small design amendments I can fold into DESIGN.md on your word.

Findings below — first what survives, then what doesn't.

## Where the design already treats the work as the work

Credit where due, because the *mechanics* mostly hold: §6's idempotency section is written from your model, not mine — re-entrancy is prework's contract, a re-pick runs over half-done work, the write ceiling bounds duplicate damage (F12/S8). F17/S31 take prework duration seriously enough to find a livelock in it. The agentless converge is a first-class exit (§6.5), `outcome:delivered` exists precisely for artifacts the work created, and the secrets path is designed around the executor phase being the operative one. The state machine, the leases, the roll — none of it assumed the work was small.

## Where the thin-work assumption leaked — four findings

What *doesn't* survive is the sizing arithmetic and the deployment coupling. Every problem below is invisible when drains take minutes and routine when they take hours.

**1. A long drain starves the tick — structural, and in the sim's blind spot.** The tick and the executor share one workflow, and ticks are serialized by a workflow-level `concurrency` group (S6 *depends* on that). A drain doing two hours of real work therefore blocks the next two hourly tick fires — instantiation, readiness flips, and the dead-claim reclaim all stall behind the very work they schedule. The reclaim riding the tick (your F4 decision, bought for ~2h recovery) quietly degrades whenever any executor is busy. Fix shape: the serialization must scope to the tick job alone (job-level concurrency) or the executor moves to its own workflow — the hourly heartbeat has to be independent of drain occupancy. The sim cannot catch this: "Tick serialization" is explicitly in the unsimulated-world table as assumed platform config.

**2. One global executing leash inflates to the heaviest task in the fleet.** F17 requires leash > every task's prework bound. Under work-as-work, a legitimate 3-hour task exists — so the leash exceeds 3h *for everyone*, and a dead executor's claim on a two-minute task also waits 3h+ to reclaim. Worse, `timeout-minutes ≤ leash` means runs may then legally run 3h, feeding finding 1. Two fix shapes: a per-task leash read from the task declaration at HEAD (the tick already reads `frequency` at HEAD for the stale rule — same move), or an executor **heartbeat comment** every ~15 minutes during work, which keeps one short global leash, makes `noActivitySince` honest, and — see visibility below — is the same mechanism the item's timeline needs anyway. I'd take the heartbeat.

**3. Throughput is executor occupancy, and §10 underprices it.** The honest capacity model: one drain run completes roughly **one heavy item** (timeout ≤ leash), and everything else waits a tick. A catch-up morning with five heavy items is a five-hour serial crawl — the CCR-parallelism I leaned on last turn is irrelevant, because the serial part is the expensive part. I retract that defusal outright. Consequences: `maxItems` and matrix width are the *primary* capacity parameters, not a one-sentence knob; the runner-concurrency budget deserves a line; and the cheap "drain until empty" continuation is self-re-dispatch (`workflow_dispatch` is one of the two events `GITHUB_TOKEN` *can* fire) rather than inflating any single run's timeout.

**4. Oldest-first plus heavy work lets one task dominate drains.** An hourly, heavy task sitting at the queue head can consume every drain's whole budget while light tasks queue behind it. At today's fleet this is a sentence, not a redesign — but it feeds directly into the next section.

- **"One run drains all items and that's fine" — wrong, retracted** (finding 3). This was the clearest place your correction bites my analysis specifically.

This is where the reframing changes the *reading* of the design's own dashboard claim ("the issue list is the scheduler's state"):

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. ## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.

content.content:
5ca4c35 Stage the executor workflow beside the tick, in one cycle (#874)
The pack update flow staged only the scheduler path, so a member flipped to
queue dispatch would receive the tick and never the executor. The two are one
mechanism split across two files: the tick creates and readies work items and
nothing else, so a member holding only the tick has a generator with no worker
— a queue that fills every hour and is never drained, which from outside is
indistinguishable from a repo whose tasks all declined.

`pendingExecutorWorkflow` is additive rather than a widening of the scheduler
lane, because the two answer different questions: every member owes a file at
the scheduler path, while a slot-dispatch member owes no executor file at all.
That null is a legitimate answer for most of the fleet and must not read as a
fault — nor, when the stub cannot be read, may "cannot answer" collapse into
"already converged", the bug the scheduler lane learned in #797.

Both errors now ride out on `detail`, joined, for the same reason the scheduler
lane chose it: a new field only reaches a member once its worker catches up a
cycle later, and `detail` reaches every fielded worker today.

Refs #801

Co-authored-by: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

 engine-tests/pack-update.test.mjs | 47 +++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++--
 updates/pack-update.mjs           | 38 +++++++++++++++++++++++++++++--
 2 files changed, 81 insertions(+), 4 deletions(-)
b30ef77 The work-item queue: the whole mechanism, canon flipped (#854)
PR-1 of the tasks-dispatch migration. Work items are issues; a thin tick gives
every recurring task a standing item at its anchor and flips blocked items ready,
and any number of executors pull from the queue — evaluating the precondition
exactly once, at pickup, and rolling the item to its next anchor on a no-go so
"asked, declined, wakes at T" lives on the item rather than in a run-ledger
watermark nobody can see.

The mechanism ships behind `taskScheduler.dispatch`, which only this repo sets to
"queue"; every member keeps the slot machinery until the fleet flip deletes it.
The two are disjoint by construction — separate issue families, separate
workflows, separate janitor sweep — so the rollback is the same config edit
backwards.

Invocation is a routine's API trigger, called ONCE per item and never retried:
the endpoint offers no idempotency key, so a retry is what would put two sessions
on one item. That single decision deleted the agent-side claim protocol rather
than simplifying it, and left an unanswered call to be settled by the janitor's
agent leash — a rule that already existed. The session's instructions are a
tracked file the routine's one-line prompt points at.

# Claudinite work-item queue — the generator tick and its drain (tasks-dispatch
# DESIGN §5, §10). This is the repo's ONLY cron, and it replaces the slot
# scheduler's content at the same path when `taskScheduler.dispatch` is `"queue"`
# — same file, same hashed minute, different mechanism, so the one-cron rule and
# every reader that knows this workflow by name keep holding.
#
# A thin shim: all logic lives in the vendored engine, so this file changes
# rarely. The minute below is a placeholder; bootstrap and the wiring converge
# rewrite it to this repo's stable hashed minute in :10–:50, computed by
# `node engine/scheduler/hash-minute.mjs <owner/repo>`.
#
# TWO JOBS, IN ORDER. The tick is pure label mechanics over the issue list —
# instantiate each task's standing item at its anchor, ready what is due, reclaim
# dead executor claims — and evaluates no precondition and collects no signal. The
# drain is an ordinary executor run: it picks up what the tick just created, which
# is what keeps the common case's latency at zero even with no `labeled` event
# delivered. Lost events are therefore never the only delivery — they are latency
# sugar, which is what retires the re-arm.
#
# `workflow_dispatch` is not a convenience: it is the never-wait-for-the-cron
# lever every forced run, migration and validation burst depends on.
name: Claudinite scheduler

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '44 * * * *'
  workflow_dispatch:

# One tick at a time, always. The tick's duplicate-standing-item self-heal is
# written assuming exactly this — it closes every open family item but the oldest,
# which is safe precisely because two ticks never run at once.
concurrency:
  group: claudinite-tick
  cancel-in-progress: false

permissions:
  contents: write        # read the repo + vendored engine; a task's prework pushes its delivery branch
  issues: write          # create / label / comment / close work items — the queue itself
  pull-requests: write   # a task's prework opens its PR and arms auto-merge
  actions: write         # dispatch a workflow a task drives (creating a workflow_dispatch event needs write; `read` silently 403s the POST)

jobs:
  tick:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Instantiate, ready and reclaim work items
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: node engine/scheduler/queue/tick.mjs

  # The post-tick drain. `timeout-minutes` MUST stay ≤ the engine's executing
  # leash (60m): a hung runner has to be killed by the platform before its claim
  # is reaped and the item re-picked, or a zombie's prework runs beside its
  # replacement's.
  drain:
    needs: tick
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 50
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Drain the queue
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          # On a member this block is stamped by the wiring converge (the
          # `# claudinite:secrets` marker in the stub); the canon has no converge,
          # so its own list is written here, by hand, in the same commit.
          FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN }}
          CCR_FLEET_ROUTINE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CCR_FLEET_ROUTINE_TOKEN }}
        run: node engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs

  # A scheduled run reaches no one when it goes red, so escalate a whole-run
  # failure to a human-visible `workflow-failure` issue. Converges to ONE open
  # issue by a fixed title (create-or-comment), and ensures the label first since a
  # first-run failure may precede any label-ensure.
  report-failure:
    needs: [tick, drain]
    if: failure()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      issues: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            const { owner, repo } = context.repo;
            const title = 'Claudinite scheduler run failed';
            await github.rest.issues.createLabel({ owner, repo, name: 'workflow-failure', color: 'b60205', description: 'Claudinite scheduler: a scheduler run or task failed' }).catch(() => {});
            const run = `${context.serverUrl}/${owner}/${repo}/actions/runs/${context.runId}`;
            const body = `The Claudinite tick/drain run failed: ${run}`;
            const found = await github.rest.search.issuesAndPullRequests({ q: `repo:${owner}/${repo} is:issue is:open in:title "${title}"` });
            if (found.data.total_count > 0) await github.rest.issues.createComment({ owner, repo, issue_number: found.data.items[0].number, body });
            else await github.rest.issues.create({ owner, repo, title, labels: ['workflow-failure'], body });

content.content:
495	   issue and that nonce.
496	
497	   **Once per item, ever — and that one decision removes a whole protocol**
498	   (owner, 2026-08-15). An earlier draft retried a timed-out call and, because
499	   a client-side timeout may still have started a session, accepted
500	   at-least-once invocation and paid for it with an agent-side claim lease
501	   (§7) to collapse the duplicates. But a retry is only safe when you know the
502	   first call did nothing, and the timeout is exactly the case where you
503	   cannot know. Declining to retry keeps invocation **at-most-once**, so two
504	   sessions can never arrive at one item and the lease has nothing to collapse.
505	   The nonce survives, earning its keep differently: it proves a fire names
506	   *this* hand-off rather than a stale or replayed one.
507	
508	   Three outcomes, and the third is the whole point:
509	   - **fired** — a session exists; the item is the agent's.
510	   - **refused** (a status came back) — no session, and the cause is a token,
511	     a URL or a routine, which no retry fixes: converge `needs-human` naming it.
512	   - **unanswered** (a timeout, a dropped connection) — the session may or may
513	     not exist, and nothing may guess. The item **stays** `task:agent` with a
514	     comment saying the outcome is unknown; whichever way it went is settled by
515	     a rule that already exists — a session that started converges the item, and
516	     one that never did leaves it silent until the janitor's agent leash (§11)
517	     brings it to triage. No new mechanism, no re-queue that could duplicate.
518	
519	   Either way a lost hand-off is a *synchronous, visible* event at the
520	   executor, not a silently missing label event (this is what retires the
521	   re-arm — §11, and the credential it costs is §12).
522	
523	An executor run may iterate (claim → … → hand off, next pick) up to a
524	configured `maxItems`; the default is a small number, and each item's claim is
525	independently leased, so executor concurrency is safe at any width. One bound
526	ties the executor to its leash ([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §2 — the
527	stalled-worker lesson): the executor job's `timeout-minutes` must be **≤ the
528	executing leash**, so a hung runner is killed by the platform before its
529	claim is reaped and re-picked — otherwise a zombie's prework runs beside its
530	replacement's.
531	
532	**Idempotency, honestly (owner concern, 2026-08-13: "I'm not sure we can
533	guarantee all tasks to be idempotent").** Agreed — and the design does not
534	require it. The queue literature's blanket "make handlers idempotent" applies
535	to systems where duplicate *invocations* reach the handler; here every
536	duplicate-invocation path collapses at a lease **before work starts** (the
537	executor claim, §6.2; the agent claim, §7), so what tasks must actually
538	tolerate is much narrower:
539	
540	- **Prework must be re-entrant** — a *sequential* re-run after a
541	  crash-and-reclaim (§6.5). That is convergence ("check what exists, continue
542	  from there"), not idempotency, and it is already required of prework today.
543	  Concurrent overlap with a zombie run is excluded by construction
544	  (`timeout-minutes` ≤ leash, above), not asked of the task.
545	- **Re-executed agent work passes through the precondition again** (§6.4),
546	  and the half-run's artifacts are on the item (Delivered section, the
547	  PR-number comments the agent posts as it works — the item is the run's own
548	  inbox/outbox). A re-pick therefore *sees* what already happened and
549	  converges `outcome:obsolete` instead of redoing it — check-before-act,
550	  carried by the mechanism, not by task-author discipline.
551	- The residual overlap cases are bounded by the **write ceiling**: the worst
552	  historical duplicate produced twin PRs — visible, closeable, never
553	  destructive.
554	
555	And for a task that can promise none of this — a genuinely one-shot side
556	effect (a store submission, an external notification, a payment-shaped
557	action): the contract gains **`on_interrupt: 'requeue' | 'needs-human'`**
558	(default `'requeue'`). Declaring `'needs-human'` makes every recovery path
559	that would re-execute — leash reclaim (§11), hand-off retry (§6.6), the

issue and that nonce.

   **Once per item, ever — and that one decision removes a whole protocol**
   (owner, 2026-08-15). An earlier draft retried a timed-out call and, because
   a client-side timeout may still have started a session, accepted
   at-least-once invocation and paid for it with an agent-side claim lease
   (§7) to collapse the duplicates. But a retry is only safe when you know the
   first call did nothing, and the timeout is exactly the case where you
   cannot know. Declining to retry keeps invocation **at-most-once**, so two
   sessions can never arrive at one item and the lease has nothing to collapse.
   The nonce survives, earning its keep differently: it proves a fire names
   *this* hand-off rather than a stale or replayed one.

   Three outcomes, and the third is the whole point:
   - **fired** — a session exists; the item is the agent's.
   - **refused** (a status came back) — no session, and the cause is a token,
     a URL or a routine, which no retry fixes: converge `needs-human` naming it.
   - **unanswered** (a timeout, a dropped connection) — the session may or may
     not exist, and nothing may guess. The item **stays** `task:agent` with a
     comment saying the outcome is unknown; whichever way it went is settled by
     a rule that already exists — a session that started converges the item, and
     one that never did leaves it silent until the janitor's agent leash (§11)
     brings it to triage. No new mechanism, no re-queue that could duplicate.

   Either way a lost hand-off is a *synchronous, visible* event at the
   executor, not a silently missing label event (this is what retires the
   re-arm — §11, and the credential it costs is §12).

An executor run may iterate (claim → … → hand off, next pick) up to a
configured `maxItems`; the default is a small number, and each item's claim is
independently leased, so executor concurrency is safe at any width. One bound
ties the executor to its leash ([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §2 — the
stalled-worker lesson): the executor job's `timeout-minutes` must be **≤ the
executing leash**, so a hung runner is killed by the platform before its
claim is reaped and re-picked — otherwise a zombie's prework runs beside its
replacement's.

**Idempotency, honestly (owner concern, 2026-08-13: "I'm not sure we can
guarantee all tasks to be idempotent").** Agreed — and the design does not
require it. The queue literature's blanket "make handlers idempotent" applies
to systems where duplicate *invocations* reach the handler; here every
duplicate-invocation path collapses at a lease **before work starts** (the
executor claim, §6.2; the agent claim, §7), so what tasks must actually
tolerate is much narrower:

- **Prework must be re-entrant** — a *sequential* re-run after a
  crash-and-reclaim (§6.5). That is convergence ("check what exists, continue
  from there"), not idempotency, and it is already required of prework today.
  Concurrent overlap with a zombie run is excluded by construction
  (`timeout-minutes` ≤ leash, above), not asked of the task.
- **Re-executed agent work passes through the precondition again** (§6.4),
  and the half-run's artifacts are on the item (Delivered section, the
  PR-number comments the agent posts as it works — the item is the run's own
  inbox/outbox). A re-pick therefore *sees* what already happened and
  converges `outcome:obsolete` instead of redoing it — check-before-act,
  carried by the mechanism, not by task-author discipline.
- The residual overlap cases are bounded by the **write ceiling**: the worst
  historical duplicate produced twin PRs — visible, closeable, never
  destructive.

And for a task that can promise none of this — a genuinely one-shot side
effect (a store submission, an external notification, a payment-shaped
action): the contract gains **`on_interrupt: 'requeue' | 'needs-human'`**
(default `'requeue'`). Declaring `'needs-human'` makes every recovery path
that would re-execute — leash reclaim (§11), hand-off retry (§6.6), the
human re-queue lever (§4) — converge to triage instead: **at-most-once plus
a human**. This is the ack-early/ack-late dial every queue exposes, and
Celery ships ack-early as its *default* precisely so non-idempotent tasks
are never silently re-run ([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §1); here the safe-side
default stays `'requeue'` because most of this fleet's tasks are
sweep-shaped, and the one-shot minority declares itself. Running
more executors — a second workflow instance, a laptop, a k8s job — requires
only an issues-scope token; nothing about the queue knows how many exist.

## 7. The agent

Today's `executor.md` collapses: the trigger-identification dance
(`resolve-dispatch`'s not-mine / scope-mismatch / no-trigger / needs-issue
verdicts, the two transports, the no-fallback rule)
existed because the session had to *discover* which label event started it. An
invoked session is told its item in its prompt — one issue number — and the
prompt is written by executor code, not by a human. What survives, verbatim in
role: validate the item in code before acting (never trust the prompt more
than a label event — re-resolve the task path at HEAD), honor the Context as
binding scope, run `task.md` at the declared model with the declared timeout
stated plainly, verify the outcome ceiling in code (`verify-outcome`), converge
the item (`outcome:done` / `outcome:delivered` / `needs-human` + comment),
print the `claudinite-task-exec` record, capture the session. One session, one
item, no queue awareness — unchanged, and now structural: the session never
receives a queue, only an item.

5. **The work step**, Action-side, unchanged contract: subprocess, task dir
   cwd, `required_secrets` as env, timeout, `CLAUDINITE_REQUEST_AGENT`
   conditional hand-off. **This step is the work, not preparation for it**
   (owner correction, 2026-08-15): for most of the fleet it is the whole task —
   long-running, crash-prone, PR-creating — and the agent phase is the
   sometimes-important judgment minority. The contract key is still spelled
   `prework` (renaming a vendored key is a migration, tracked separately);
   the design calls the phase what it is. Three requirements, the first
   stated explicitly since SCENARIOS S8/F12:
   - **Re-entrant** — a dead executor's claim is reclaimed and the item
     re-picked, so the work can run again over its own half-done output (it
     already must survive this today, where a scheduler run dying mid-work
     leaves the slot due; the contract just never said so).
   - **Heartbeat while it runs** (work-as-work review, 2026-08-15): the
     executor comments on the item every ~15 minutes during the work step.
     The heartbeat is what lets one short global executing leash survive
     arbitrarily long work — the leash measures executor *death* (heartbeats
     stopped), never work *duration* — and it is the item's visibility during
     the hours its timeline would otherwise go dark (§11 has the leash
     arithmetic this replaces).
   - **The terminal comment is the durable record.** Actions logs expire; the
     item is what remains. Whatever ends the item — converge here, or the
     agent later — the closing comment carries the `claudinite-task-exec`
     record and every artifact the work created (PR links above all). For an
     agentless task this comment is the *only* durable trace of the run, which
     is what makes it non-optional.

   done — the quiet-on-success property survives as a *closed* item rather
   than no item, which is the better trade: the run is now visible.

An executor run may iterate (claim → … → hand off, next pick) up to a
configured `maxItems`; the default is a small number, and each item's claim is
independently leased, so executor concurrency is safe at any width. The old
bound tying the run to its leash — `timeout-minutes` ≤ the executing leash, so
the platform killed a hung runner before its claim was reaped — **retires with
the heartbeat** (2026-08-15): it capped every run at under an hour, which the
work-as-work model cannot accept. The stalled-worker lesson
([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §2) is now held by three smaller pieces instead: a
*dead* runner stops heartbeating and is reclaimed within ~the leash; a *wedged
work subprocess* is killed by the work's own declared timeout (the contract's
existing bound), after which the executor converges the failure; and a
*reclaimed-but-alive* runner abandons at its next transition, because the
executor re-verifies its own lease at every state change (§11). The run's
`timeout-minutes` is then sized to the work it may legally do — `maxItems` ×
the largest work bound it can pick — not to the leash.

An executor run may iterate (claim → … → hand off, next pick) up to a
configured `maxItems`; the default is a small number, and each item's claim is
independently leased, so executor concurrency is safe at any width. The old
bound tying the run to its leash — `timeout-minutes` ≤ the executing leash, so
the platform killed a hung runner before its claim was reaped — **retires with
the heartbeat** (2026-08-15): it capped every run at under an hour, which the
work-as-work model cannot accept. The stalled-worker lesson
([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §2) is now held by three smaller pieces instead: a
*dead* runner stops heartbeating and is reclaimed within ~the leash; a *wedged
work subprocess* is killed by the work's own declared timeout (the contract's
existing bound), after which the executor converges the failure; and a
*reclaimed-but-alive* runner abandons at its next transition, because the
executor re-verifies its own lease at every state change (§11). The run's
`timeout-minutes` is then sized to the work it may legally do — `maxItems` ×
the largest work bound it can pick — not to the leash.

input.new_string:
**Readiness has a second site: whoever closes an item re-checks its dependents
in code** (F1, reopened by the owner 2026-08-15 — reversing the 2026-08-13
decline, and amending §15.8's "dependency readiness is the tick's alone" in
siting, not in principle). On closing an item, the executor or agent doing the
closing evaluates every open `task:blocked` item naming it: `Blocked-by` all
closed and `Not-before` passed flips the dependent to `task:ready`, and a
drain follows — so a chain link or a fan-in proceeds within minutes of its
upstream converging instead of waiting out the tick. What changed since the
decline: under the work-as-work model the ~1h/link quantization stacks on
drain occupancy, so a three-link chain on a busy morning trailed into the
afternoon. The tick's readiness job stays exactly as it was, as the backstop —
a close by hand runs no engine code, and a missed re-check costs a tick of
latency, never correctness (SCENARIOS S33, and S4's tightened chain timing).

735	free ([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §2). The body fields remain the truth the tick
736	parses — they are portable to any tracker with issues, labels, and comments,
737	which is the platform-agnosticism the sketch asks for. One vendored module owns
738	parse/serialize of the two fields; nothing else touches them.
739	
740	Cycles: the tick readies nothing in a `Blocked-by` cycle, forever, and the
741	stale escalation (§11) surfaces it as `needs-human` after ~2 periods — the
742	same convergence-not-prevention posture as the rest of the system. The tick
743	does not attempt cycle detection; the janitor's health review may.
744	
745	## 10. Capacity and platform-agnosticism
746	
747	The default deployment stays one vendored workflow — the repo's only cron,
748	rule unchanged — now containing the tick job and one executor job (the tick
749	runs first; the executor drains what it created, which keeps the common case's
750	latency at zero even without events). Event triggers (`task:ready` labeled)
751	give urgent and hand-created items sub-minute pickup. Scaling is a config
752	knob: the executor job's `maxItems`, a matrix width for parallel executor
753	jobs, or executors outside Actions entirely — the executor contract is "issue
754	read/write plus the repo checkout at HEAD", so a runner anywhere with a token
755	qualifies. Executor identity is self-declared in claim comments; the system
756	never enumerates executors, which is why adding one requires telling no one.
757	
758	## 11. Recovery — what the janitor keeps, what dies
759	
760	| failure | today | proposed |
761	|---|---|---|
762	| scheduler/tick miss or late fire | run-ledger catch-up math | same property from the occurrence guard (§5) — the next tick instantiates the most recent occurrence only |
763	| double tick | concurrency group + slot-title search | concurrency group + occurrence-guard search (same window, same answer) |
764	| lost label event | janitor re-arm (remove/re-add), 20-min grace, bounded by stale escalation | **retired** — executors poll on the tick's cron; events are latency sugar, never the only delivery |

parses — they are portable to any tracker with issues, labels, and comments,
which is the platform-agnosticism the sketch asks for. One vendored module owns
parse/serialize of the two fields; nothing else touches them.

Cycles: the tick readies nothing in a `Blocked-by` cycle, forever, and the
stale escalation (§11) surfaces it as `needs-human` after ~2 periods — the
same convergence-not-prevention posture as the rest of the system. The tick
does not attempt cycle detection; the janitor's health review may.

## 10. Capacity and platform-agnosticism

The default deployment stays one vendored workflow — the repo's only cron,
rule unchanged — now containing the tick job and one executor job (the tick
runs first; the executor drains what it created, which keeps the common case's
latency at zero even without events). Event triggers (`task:ready` labeled)
give urgent and hand-created items sub-minute pickup. Scaling is a config
knob: the executor job's `maxItems`, a matrix width for parallel executor
jobs, or executors outside Actions entirely — the executor contract is "issue
read/write plus the repo checkout at HEAD", so a runner anywhere with a token
qualifies. Executor identity is self-declared in claim comments; the system
never enumerates executors, which is why adding one requires telling no one.

## 11. Recovery — what the janitor keeps, what dies

| failure | today | proposed |
|---|---|---|
| scheduler/tick miss or late fire | run-ledger catch-up math | same property from the occurrence guard (§5) — the next tick instantiates the most recent occurrence only |
| double tick | concurrency group + slot-title search | concurrency group + occurrence-guard search (same window, same answer) |
| lost label event | janitor re-arm (remove/re-add), 20-min grace, bounded by stale escalation | **retired** — executors poll on the tick's cron; events are latency sugar, never the only delivery |

## 10. Capacity and platform-agnosticism

The default deployment stays one vendored cron workflow — the repo's only
cron, rule unchanged — containing the tick job and a drain (the tick runs
first; the executor drains what it created, which keeps the common case's
latency at zero even without events). Event triggers (`task:ready` labeled)
give urgent and hand-created items sub-minute pickup — with one platform fact
worth knowing: a label written by a workflow's own `GITHUB_TOKEN` emits no
triggering event (GitHub's recursion guard), so events only ever come from
*foreign* tokens — a human, a CLI on a PAT, an agent session. The drain being
in-run is what makes that harmless; it is the structural delivery, events the
sugar.

**The capacity model, honestly** (work-as-work review, 2026-08-15): the work
step is the work, so a drain's throughput is its *occupancy* — one run
completes roughly `maxItems` heavy items serially, and everything it leaves
waits a tick. The CCR sessions it hands off parallelize for free; the
executor-side work does not. So `maxItems` and executor width are the primary
capacity parameters, not a garnish: scale with a matrix width for parallel
executor jobs (shipping the randomized after-urgent pick order in the same
change, §6.1), with executors outside Actions entirely — the contract is
"issue read/write plus the repo checkout at HEAD", so a runner anywhere with a
token qualifies — and, for the drain-until-empty shape without inflating any
one run, with **self-re-dispatch**: `workflow_dispatch` is one of the two
event types a `GITHUB_TOKEN` *can* fire, so a drain that exits with ready
items left re-dispatches the executor workflow and lets a fresh run continue.
One fairness note, accepted at today's scale: oldest-first plus heavy work
lets one task's item dominate a drain's whole budget while light tasks queue
behind it — a sentence here rather than machinery, until it is measured.

**The tick must never wait on a drain** (work-as-work review, 2026-08-15).
The heartbeat retires the sub-hour cap on executor runs (§6), and a long
drain sharing the tick's serializing `concurrency` group would then hold the
next cron fire — instantiation, readiness and the leash reclaim all stalling
behind the very work they schedule. So the serialization the double-tick
guard needs (S6) scopes to the **tick alone**, and executor work runs outside
it: the drain leaves the cron workflow's concurrency group (its own group, or
the separate executor workflow via dispatch). A deployment where the drain
can still block the tick is mis-wired even while nothing visibly fails.

Executor identity is self-declared in claim comments; the system never
enumerates executors, which is why adding one requires telling no one.

Two leash constraints, made explicit by the validation review (2026-08-13) and
the first **reframed by the work-as-work review (2026-08-15)**:

- **The executing leash measures executor death, never work duration — the
  heartbeat is what buys that (F17, reframed).** As first written, F17 made
  the leash exceed every task's work bound, which under the work-as-work model
  inflates it to the heaviest task in the fleet: one legitimate three-hour
  task and a dead executor on a two-minute task also waits three hours to
  reclaim. Instead the executor **comments a heartbeat on the item every ~15
  minutes during the work step** (§6.5): a live run is never reclaimed however
  long it works (S31c), a dead one stops heartbeating and is reclaimed within

Steps 2–3 and 6–8's storage half are Actions-platform behavior the simulator
deliberately does not model (prose rows in the coverage map); the
needs-human convergence postures are ordinary sim territory.

### Migration

Deliberately thin here — **the phase plan lives in the tracking issue,
[#801](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/801)** (two PRs, two
approval points, one same-day validation burst) — with this record keeping
only the property that makes it tractable: the two
mechanisms coexist per-repo behind `taskScheduler.dispatch:
"slots" | "queue"`, sharing the task contract, with disjoint issue families
(`[claudinite-task]` vs `[claudinite-work]`) — so the flip is a config edit
and the rollback is the same edit backwards, with each mechanism's open
items untouched by the other. Every retired slot mechanism deletes in the
same PR that lands its replacement's fleet flip. One known migration detail
(SCENARIOS F8): the signal collectors' self-trigger exclusions must learn
the new vocabulary before the first queue-mode repo flips, or the queue's
own items read as repo activity to the preconditions watching it.

## 15. Decisions on record (owner, 2026-08-13)

The eight questions this design opened, as answered. Where an answer changed
the design rather than confirming it, the section it changed is named.

1. **Invocation is a CCR API call** (§12). Reverses per-project-scheduling
   §12.6; the session-creation credential in every repo is an accepted cost.
2. **The precondition re-runs at pickup, and forcing loses its exemption**
   (§6.4) — conditioned on preconditions asking task questions, not calendar
   ones. #515's rationale does not survive the pull model.
3. **Timing in a precondition is advisory, not forbidden** (§6.4): permitted
   where the verdict cannot flip between creation and pickup for scheduling
   reasons alone. No check — the property is not mechanically checkable, and
   the residual failure is a visible `outcome:obsolete`, not a wrong result.
4. **A precondition is go/no-go, never maybe-later** (§5) — *changed the
   design twice*. First cut: one verdict per occurrence at the first tick
   after the anchor, which required a `lastTick` read from the Actions ledger
   — a partial rebuild of the very watermark §1 complains about, called out
   as such when the owner asked for a state assessment. Resolved by the
   owner's **standing-item model** (decision 13 below): the verdict stays
   once-per-period, and the memory moves onto the item itself (`Not-before`
   roll), deleting the ledger read entirely. Mid-window firing stays out; a
   task wanting finer latency declares a finer `frequency`.
5. **The fleet concept is eliminated** (§12, §13) — *changed the design*.
   Wider reach is a different invocation endpoint, declared by the task that
   needs it. `ready-for-agent-fleet`, the second executor routine, and
   `session_scope` all delete. (One elaboration flagged in §12: the task names
   an endpoint *key*, with the URL and credential in repo config, so no
   vendored pack file carries deployment detail.)
6. **The executing-leash reclaim rides the tick** (§11) — *changed the
   design*. ~2h to recover a dead executor's item instead of ~25h; the janitor
   keeps the judgment sweeps. Amends the 2026-08-06 single-recovery-site split
   in siting, not in principle.
7. **Namespaced labels, executor identity in claim comments** (§4). As
   drafted; the sketch's literals and a label-per-executor are both declined —
   the first for queryability, the second because executor identities are an
   unbounded set.
8. **Dependency readiness is the tick's alone** (§9). No converger poke: one
   site evaluates `Blocked-by`/`Not-before`, and ~1h per chain link is within
   what nightly work tolerates.

Standing entries — no decision needed now:

9. **Known limitation (S18):** a fan-in blocked on a stuck child waits for a
   human; no quorum or deadline semantics at this scale. The janitor's stale
   escalation is the visibility. Revisit only on evidence.

The work-as-work review (owner, 2026-08-15). The correcting premise, in the
owner's words: *"The pre work is not pre work. It's work. Sometimes there's
also agentic work. The work can take time. The work can crash. The work
creates PRs. The work is a lot."* Every sizing assumption in the design was
re-derived under it — the mechanics survived; the arithmetic and the
deployment coupling did not:

14. **The work step is the work** (§6.5) — the executor-side subprocess is the
    whole task for most of the fleet; the agent phase is the judgment
    minority. The design names the phase **the work step**; the vendored
    contract key stays spelled `prework` until its own rename migration
    (tracked in the follow-up issue), because renaming a key every member's
    files carry is a fleet migration, not a doc edit.
15. **Heartbeat comments during the work step** (§6.5, §11) — *changed the
    design*: F17 reframed (heartbeat interval < leash replaces leash >
    every work bound), the `timeout-minutes ≤ leash` run cap retired (§6),
    and the item's timeline stays live through long work. One mechanism
    serves recovery and visibility.
16. **The tick never waits on a drain** (§10) — *changed the design*: the
    double-tick serialization scopes to the tick alone; executor work runs
    outside that concurrency group, or the heartbeat's legal long runs would
    starve the hourly tick behind the platform's queueing.
17. **The occupancy capacity model** (§10): a drain's throughput is its
    serial work-step occupancy, so `maxItems` and executor width are the
    primary capacity parameters; self-re-dispatch (`workflow_dispatch`, one
    of the two events a `GITHUB_TOKEN` can fire) is the drain-until-empty
    shape; the oldest-first fairness exposure is named and accepted at
    today's scale.
18. **The terminal comment is the durable record** (§6.5): the
    `claudinite-task-exec` record and every artifact the work created land on
    the item at close — Actions logs expire, and for agentless runs (the
    majority, under this review's premise) the item is the only durable trace.
19. **F1 reopened — readiness re-checks at close** (§9), amending decision 8
    in siting, not principle: whoever closes an item readies its dependents in
    code and a drain follows; the tick stays the backstop. (S33, S4.)
20. **Randomized pick order ships with executor width, not before** (§6.1,
    §10): at width 1 it is a no-op; at width >1 the oldest-first head
    collision cascade justifies it, in the same change.
21. **"Tick" keeps its name for now** — the owner's naming rule (spell names
    out; no single nouns that need contextual reading) applies to everything
    new here ("the work step", "the readiness re-check at close", "heartbeat
    comments"), and renaming the tick itself is deferred to
    [#877](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/877) so it lands
    after the old slot scheduler's vocabulary retires and the
    "scheduler"-name collision is moot.

## Findings ledger
input.new_string:
## I. The work-as-work review (owner corrections, 2026-08-15)

Two owner rulings landed the same day, and this section replays what they
touch. First the **invocation reversal** (recorded in DESIGN §6.6/§7/§15.11
when the mechanism was built): the routine-fire endpoint has no idempotency
key, and the owner's correction was *don't create the duplicates* — one call
per item, never retried, so at-least-once invocation, the hand-off retry (F3)
and the agent-side claim lease (F5) all delete. Then the **work-as-work
correction**: *"The pre work is not pre work. It's work. Sometimes there's
also agentic work. The work can take time. The work can crash. The work
creates PRs. The work is a lot."* The executor-side work step is the whole
task for most of the fleet; every sizing assumption built on "the drain is
quick" was re-derived. The simulator was brought up to both in this same
change — the sections below supersede S9/S10/S31 as previously written.

### S9/S10, replayed under at-most-once invocation

- **S9a (refused)**: the endpoint answers with an error — a token, URL or
  routine is wrong, which no retry fixes. The item converges `needs-human` at
  once, naming the cause; zero sessions exist. (Replaces the bounded
  revert-and-retry of F3, which assumed retrying was safe.)
- **S10a (unanswered, session started)**: the call times out client-side but
  did create a session. Nothing retries — so exactly one session exists, and
  it converges the item itself. The duplicate-session problem F5's lease
  solved can no longer occur.
- **S10b (unanswered, no session)**: the call created nothing. The item stays
  `task:agent` wearing the outcome-unknown comment, silent, until the
  janitor's agent leash brings it to triage within hours. The cost of never
  guessing is bounded latency on a rare platform failure — the trade the
  owner chose over any path that could put two sessions on one item.

### S31, replayed under the heartbeat (F20 — the leash inflation)

F17 as first written made the executing leash exceed every task's work bound —
which, once the work step is priced as the work, inflates the leash to the
heaviest task in the fleet and slows every dead-executor recovery to match.
The heartbeat replaces that arithmetic:

- **S31**: the wiring check shrinks to the one relation the heartbeat needs —
  interval well inside the leash; a violating configuration is refused at
  construction.
- **S31b**: with heartbeats switched off, the original livelock is still
  demonstrable — a silent long work step is reclaimed alive every cycle,
  re-executes forever, never converges. This is why the heartbeat is
  contract, not courtesy.
- **S31c**: a 130-minute work step heartbeats through two leash windows, is
  never reclaimed, and converges once — long work is now legal.
- **S31d**: the runner dies 40 minutes into that work; heartbeats stop, and
  the reclaim lands within ~leash of the last heartbeat — recovery is bounded
  by the leash, never by the work's duration. The re-pick converges (the work
  step's re-entrancy contract, F12, unchanged).

### S33 — the readiness re-check at close (F1, reopened)

Two fan-out members converge; the close of the second readies the fan-in **in
code, within the minute**, and the follow-on drain runs it — no tick in the
path (`ready` carries `by: close`). S4 gains the matching assertion on the
yield side: the chain's dependent is picked within minutes of its upstream
closing. A close by hand still runs no engine code; S18 keeps the tick as
that path's backstop, unchanged.

### The prose-only findings (no scenario can carry them)

- **F19 — a long drain starves the tick.** The drain job shares the cron
  workflow's serializing `concurrency` group, so once the heartbeat legalizes
  multi-hour work, a busy drain holds the next hourly fire — instantiation,
  readiness and the leash reclaim all stall behind the very work they
  schedule. Fixed in DESIGN §10: the serialization scopes to the tick alone;
  executor work runs outside it. The sim cannot see workflow concurrency
  (unsimulated-world row); the migration burst verifies the wiring.
- **F21 — throughput was priced as if drains were free.** A drain's real
  throughput is its serial work-step occupancy; `maxItems` and executor width
  are the primary capacity parameters, with self-re-dispatch as the
  drain-until-empty shape and the oldest-first fairness exposure named and
  accepted. DESIGN §10 carries the model.
- **F22 — the durable record was implicit.** Actions logs expire; for an
  agentless run — the majority, under this review's premise — the item's
  terminal comment is the only durable trace, so it must carry the
  `claudinite-task-exec` record and every artifact the work created. DESIGN
  §6.5 makes it contract.

creates PRs. The work is a lot."* The executor-side work step is the whole
task for most of the fleet; every sizing assumption built on "the drain is
quick" was re-derived. The simulator was brought up to both in this same
change — the sections below supersede S9/S10/S31 as previously written.

### S9/S10, replayed under at-most-once invocation

- **S9a (refused)**: the endpoint answers with an error — a token, URL or
  routine is wrong, which no retry fixes. The item converges `needs-human` at
  once, naming the cause; zero sessions exist. (Replaces the bounded
  revert-and-retry of F3, which assumed retrying was safe.)
- **S10a (unanswered, session started)**: the call times out client-side but
  did create a session. Nothing retries — so exactly one session exists, and
  it converges the item itself. The duplicate-session problem F5's lease
  solved can no longer occur.
- **S10b (unanswered, no session)**: the call created nothing. The item stays
  `task:agent` wearing the outcome-unknown comment, silent, until the
  janitor's agent leash brings it to triage within hours. The cost of never
  guessing is bounded latency on a rare platform failure — the trade the
  owner chose over any path that could put two sessions on one item.

### S31, replayed under the heartbeat (F20 — the leash inflation)

F17 as first written made the executing leash exceed every task's work bound —
which, once the work step is priced as the work, inflates the leash to the
heaviest task in the fleet and slows every dead-executor recovery to match.
The heartbeat replaces that arithmetic:

- **S31**: the wiring check shrinks to the one relation the heartbeat needs —
  interval well inside the leash; a violating configuration is refused at
  construction.
- **S31b**: with heartbeats switched off, the original livelock is still
  demonstrable — a silent long work step is reclaimed alive every cycle,
  re-executes forever, never converges. This is why the heartbeat is
  contract, not courtesy.
- **S31c**: a 130-minute work step heartbeats through two leash windows, is
  never reclaimed, and converges once — long work is now legal.
- **S31d**: the runner dies 40 minutes into that work; heartbeats stop, and
  the reclaim lands within ~leash of the last heartbeat — recovery is bounded
  by the leash, never by the work's duration. The re-pick converges (the work
  step's re-entrancy contract, F12, unchanged).

### S33 — the readiness re-check at close (F1, reopened)

Two fan-out members converge; the close of the second readies the fan-in **in
code, within the minute**, and the follow-on drain runs it — no tick in the
path (`ready` carries `by: close`). S4 gains the matching assertion on the
yield side: the chain's dependent is picked within minutes of its upstream
closing. A close by hand still runs no engine code; S18 keeps the tick as
that path's backstop, unchanged.

### The prose-only findings (no scenario can carry them)

- **F19 — a long drain starves the tick.** The drain job shares the cron
  workflow's serializing `concurrency` group, so once the heartbeat legalizes
  multi-hour work, a busy drain holds the next hourly fire — instantiation,
  readiness and the leash reclaim all stall behind the very work they
  schedule. Fixed in DESIGN §10: the serialization scopes to the tick alone;
  executor work runs outside it. The sim cannot see workflow concurrency
  (unsimulated-world row); the migration burst verifies the wiring.
- **F21 — throughput was priced as if drains were free.** A drain's real
  throughput is its serial work-step occupancy; `maxItems` and executor width
  are the primary capacity parameters, with self-re-dispatch as the
  drain-until-empty shape and the oldest-first fairness exposure named and
  accepted. DESIGN §10 carries the model.
- **F22 — the durable record was implicit.** Actions logs expire; for an
  agentless run — the majority, under this review's premise — the item's
  terminal comment is the only durable trace, so it must carry the
  `claudinite-task-exec` record and every artifact the work created. DESIGN
  §6.5 makes it contract.

+## I. The work-as-work review (owner corrections, 2026-08-15)
+
+Two owner rulings landed the same day, and this section replays what they
+touch. First the **invocation reversal** (recorded in DESIGN §6.6/§7/§15.11
+when the mechanism was built): the routine-fire endpoint has no idempotency
+key, and the owner's correction was *don't create the duplicates* — one call
+per item, never retried, so at-least-once invocation, the hand-off retry (F3)
+and the agent-side claim lease (F5) all delete. Then the **work-as-work
+correction**: *"The pre work is not pre work. It's work. Sometimes there's
+also agentic work. The work can take time. The work can crash. The work
+creates PRs. The work is a lot."* The executor-side work step is the whole
+task for most of the fleet; every sizing assumption built on "the drain is
+quick" was re-derived. The simulator was brought up to both in this same
+change — the sections below supersede S9/S10/S31 as previously written.
+
+### S9/S10, replayed under at-most-once invocation
+
+- **S9a (refused)**: the endpoint answers with an error — a token, URL or
+  routine is wrong, which no retry fixes. The item converges `needs-human` at
+  once, naming the cause; zero sessions exist. (Replaces the bounded
+  revert-and-retry of F3, which assumed retrying was safe.)
+- **S10a (unanswered, session started)**: the call times out client-side but
+  did create a session. Nothing retries — so exactly one session exists, and
+  it converges the item itself. The duplicate-session problem F5's lease
+  solved can no longer occur.
+- **S10b (unanswered, no session)**: the call created nothing. The item stays
+  `task:agent` wearing the outcome-unknown comment, silent, until the
+  janitor's agent leash brings it to triage within hours. The cost of never
+  guessing is bounded latency on a rare platform failure — the trade the
+  owner chose over any path that could put two sessions on one item.
+
+### S31, replayed under the heartbeat (F20 — the leash inflation)
+
+F17 as first written made the executing leash exceed every task's work bound —
+which, once the work step is priced as the work, inflates the leash to the
+heaviest task in the fleet and slows every dead-executor recovery to match.
+The heartbeat replaces that arithmetic:
+
+- **S31**: the wiring check shrinks to the one relation the heartbeat needs —
+  interval well inside the leash; a violating configuration is refused at
+  construction.
+- **S31b**: with heartbeats switched off, the original livelock is still
+  demonstrable — a silent long work step is reclaimed alive every cycle,
+  re-executes forever, never converges. This is why the heartbeat is
+  contract, not courtesy.
+- **S31c**: a 130-minute work step heartbeats through two leash windows, is
+  never reclaimed, and converges once — long work is now legal.
+- **S31d**: the runner dies 40 minutes into that work; heartbeats stop, and
+  the reclaim lands within ~leash of the last heartbeat — recovery is bounded
+  by the leash, never by the work's duration. The re-pick converges (the work
+  step's re-entrancy contract, F12, unchanged).
+
+### S33 — the readiness re-check at close (F1, reopened)
+
+Two fan-out members converge; the close of the second readies the fan-in **in
+code, within the minute**, and the follow-on drain runs it — no tick in the
+path (`ready` carries `by: close`). S4 gains the matching assertion on the
+yield side: the chain's dependent is picked within minutes of its upstream
+closing. A close by hand still runs no engine code; S18 keeps the tick as
+that path's backstop, unchanged.
+
+### The prose-only findings (no scenario can carry them)
+
+- **F19 — a long drain starves the tick.** The drain job shares the cron
+  workflow's serializing `concurrency` group, so once the heartbeat legalizes
+  multi-hour work, a busy drain holds the next hourly fire — instantiation,
+  readiness and the leash reclaim all stall behind the very work they
+  schedule. Fixed in DESIGN §10: the serialization scopes to the tick alone;
+  executor work runs outside it. The sim cannot see workflow concurrency
+  (unsimulated-world row); the migration burst verifies the wiring.
+- **F21 — throughput was priced as if drains were free.** A drain's real
+  throughput is its serial work-step occupancy; `maxItems` and executor width
+  are the primary capacity parameters, with self-re-dispatch as the
+  drain-until-empty shape and the oldest-first fairness exposure named and
+  accepted. DESIGN §10 carries the model.
+- **F22 — the durable record was implicit.** Actions logs expire; for an
+  agentless run — the majority, under this review's premise — the item's
+  terminal comment is the only durable trace, so it must carry the
+  `claudinite-task-exec` record and every artifact the work created. DESIGN
+  §6.5 makes it contract.

+  revert-and-retry of F3, which assumed retrying was safe.)

+  did create a session. Nothing retries — so exactly one session exists, and
+  it converges the item itself. The duplicate-session problem F5's lease
+  solved can no longer occur.
+- **S10b (unanswered, no session)**: the call created nothing. The item stays
+  `task:agent` wearing the outcome-unknown comment, silent, until the
+  janitor's agent leash brings it to triage within hours. The cost of never
+  guessing is bounded latency on a rare platform failure — the trade the
+  owner chose over any path that could put two sessions on one item.
+
+### S31, replayed under the heartbeat (F20 — the leash inflation)
+
+F17 as first written made the executing leash exceed every task's work bound —
+which, once the work step is priced as the work, inflates the leash to the
+heaviest task in the fleet and slows every dead-executor recovery to match.
+The heartbeat replaces that arithmetic:
+
+- **S31**: the wiring check shrinks to the one relation the heartbeat needs —
+  interval well inside the leash; a violating configuration is refused at
+  construction.
+- **S31b**: with heartbeats switched off, the original livelock is still
+  demonstrable — a silent long work step is reclaimed alive every cycle,
+  re-executes forever, never converges. This is why the heartbeat is
+  contract, not courtesy.
+- **S31c**: a 130-minute work step heartbeats through two leash windows, is
+  never reclaimed, and converges once — long work is now legal.
+- **S31d**: the runner dies 40 minutes into that work; heartbeats stop, and
+  the reclaim lands within ~leash of the last heartbeat — recovery is bounded
+  by the leash, never by the work's duration. The re-pick converges (the work
+  step's re-entrancy contract, F12, unchanged).

+
+Two fan-out members converge; the close of the second readies the fan-in **in
+code, within the minute**, and the follow-on drain runs it — no tick in the
+path (`ready` carries `by: close`). S4 gains the matching assertion on the
+yield side: the chain's dependent is picked within minutes of its upstream
+closing. A close by hand still runs no engine code; S18 keeps the tick as
+that path's backstop, unchanged.

+  workflow's serializing `concurrency` group, so once the heartbeat legalizes

+  readiness and the leash reclaim all stall behind the very work they

+  executor work runs outside it. The sim cannot see workflow concurrency

+  throughput is its serial work-step occupancy; `maxItems` and executor width
+  are the primary capacity parameters, with self-re-dispatch as the
+  drain-until-empty shape and the oldest-first fairness exposure named and
+  accepted. DESIGN §10 carries the model.
+- **F22 — the durable record was implicit.** Actions logs expire; for an
+  agentless run — the majority, under this review's premise — the item's
+  terminal comment is the only durable trace, so it must carry the
+  `claudinite-task-exec` record and every artifact the work created. DESIGN
+  §6.5 makes it contract.

content.text: Now the follow-up issue for the engine-side implementation of what the design now requires:

input.title: queue engine: implement the work-as-work amendments (heartbeat, tick/drain decoupling, self-re-dispatch, durable record, readiness re-check at close, prework key rename)
input.body:
The work-as-work review (#876) landed in the design docs and the simulator; `engine/scheduler/queue/` still implements the pre-review contract. Until each box below lands, the design describes behavior the engine does not yet have:

- [ ] **Heartbeat comments** — the executor comments on the item every ~15 min during the work step (`prework-run.mjs` / `executor.mjs`); the tick's leash reclaim then measures heartbeat silence. While off: long work is illegal (the leash/timeout arithmetic caps runs under an hour) and items go dark during work.
- [ ] **Retire `timeout-minutes ≤ leash`** in both workflow comments once the heartbeat lands; size run timeouts to `maxItems` × the largest work bound. (DESIGN §6.)
- [ ] **Tick/drain decoupling** — the drain job must leave the cron workflow's `claudinite-tick` concurrency group (own group, or the executor workflow via dispatch). While off: a multi-hour drain starves the hourly tick (F19) — currently masked only by the 50m timeout the heartbeat retires.
- [ ] **Self-re-dispatch** — a drain exiting with ready items left `workflow_dispatch`es the executor workflow (`GITHUB_TOKEN` can fire it). While off: leftover items wait a tick each.
- [ ] **Durable record** — the terminal comment carries the `claudinite-task-exec` record + artifact links (agentless runs especially). While off: an agentless run's only record expires with its Actions log.
- [ ] **Readiness re-check at close (F1)** — executor/agent close paths ready dependents whose `Blocked-by`/`Not-before` now hold, then trigger a drain; tick stays the backstop. While off: chain links wait ~1h each.
- [ ] **Rename the `prework` contract key to match the design's "work step" vocabulary** — a fleet migration (vendored key in every member's task files); ship with a compatibility window per the updates/* skew rules. While off: harmless naming skew, documented in DESIGN §6.5/§15.14.

Wiring conformance: heartbeat interval < executing leash (the reframed F17 check) belongs beside the existing wiring checks.

Blocked by the docs/sim PR for #876. Closing condition: every box implemented with tests, the design's §6/§10/§11 statements true of a real run.

input.body:
The owner's correction (2026-08-15): **the work step is the work** — long-running, crash-prone, PR-creating, often the whole task — and the agent phase is the judgment minority. Every sizing assumption in the tasks-dispatch design was re-derived under it; the mechanics survived, the arithmetic and the deployment coupling did not. This PR lands the review's decisions (DESIGN §15.14–21, sim-first) in docs + simulator; the engine implementation is tracked in #883.

**Decisions folded in:**
- **Heartbeat comments during the work step** (§6.5/§11) — the executing leash measures executor *death*, never work *duration*; F17's wiring check reframed to heartbeat interval < leash; the `timeout-minutes ≤ leash` run cap retires (F20; S31/S31b/S31c/S31d).
- **The tick never waits on a drain** (§10) — the double-tick serialization scopes to the tick job alone; a long drain sharing the group would starve the hourly tick (F19).
- **The occupancy capacity model** (§10) — a drain's throughput is its serial work-step occupancy: `maxItems`/executor width as primary capacity parameters, self-re-dispatch via `workflow_dispatch` for drain-until-empty, the oldest-first fairness exposure named (F21).
- **The terminal comment is the durable record** (§6.5) — exec record + artifact links on the item; for agentless runs it is the only durable trace (F22).
- **F1 reopened** (§9, amending §15.8) — whoever closes an item re-checks its dependents' readiness in code, a drain follows; the tick stays the backstop (S33, and S4's tightened chain timing).
- **Randomized pick order ships with executor width, not before** (§6.1/§10).
- **The phase is named "the work step"** — the vendored `prework` contract key keeps its spelling until its own migration (#883); "tick" keeps its name for now (#877).

**Also:** brings SCENARIOS.md and the simulator up to the **at-most-once invocation reversal** that #854 recorded in DESIGN but not in the sim — S9a/S10a/S10b (refused/unanswered-started/unanswered-dead) replace the retry-and-lease machinery; F3/F5 marked superseded in the findings ledger.

**Verification:** sim suite 42/42 (new scenarios S31c/S31d/S33, rewritten S9/S10/S31), full tracked suite 1768/1768, conformance sweep 0 blocking.

Refs #876. Follow-ups: #883 (engine implementation), #877 (tick rename, blocked by #801).

Yes — the sim was changed first, and every behavior change carries a test. Concretely, in [PR #884](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/884):

**Simulator changes ([sim.mjs](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/tasks-dispatch-design-analysis-mxj7x6/docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/sim.mjs)):**
- **Heartbeats**: during the work step the executor now bumps the item's activity every `heartbeatMinutes` (default 15), guarded by the same "is my claim still this episode's newest" check as the completion path. The F17 constructor check changed from `work bound < leash` (which would now be wrong) to `heartbeat interval < leash`, and `heartbeatsDisabled` exists solely so the livelock the heartbeat prevents stays demonstrable.
- **Crash-mid-work**: a new `crashDuringWorkOf(taskId, minutes)` lever — heartbeats fire until the death, then stop, so the reclaim-from-last-heartbeat property is testable.
- **Readiness re-check at close (F1)**: `close()` now readies any blocked item whose `Blocked-by`/`Not-before` hold and schedules a drain; `ready` log events carry `by: 'close'` so tests can distinguish the closing side from the tick. Hand closes (`closeByHand`) deliberately don't do this — the tick backstop covers them, matching the design.
- **At-most-once invocation** (the #854 reconciliation): `handOff` fires once, ever — refused → `needs-human`, unanswered → item stays `task:agent` with `apiUnansweredOnce({started})` modeling both sub-cases. The retry counter, `apiTimeoutOnce`, and the whole `agentClaims` lease machinery were deleted.

**Tests ([scenarios.test.mjs](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/tasks-dispatch-design-analysis-mxj7x6/docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/scenarios.test.mjs)):**
- **New**: S31c (130-minute work heartbeats through two leash windows, zero reclaims, converges once), S31d (executor dies 40 minutes into long work → reclaimed within ~leash of the last heartbeat, not the work bound, then re-picked and converged), S33 (fan-in readied within the minute of its last blocker's close, `by: 'close'`, runs minutes later).
- **Rewritten**: S31 (wiring check now refuses heartbeat ≥ leash), S31b (livelock demo via `heartbeatsDisabled`), S9a (refused → immediate `needs-human`, zero sessions), S10a/S10b (unanswered with/without a real session — exactly one session ever, or the janitor's agent leash sweeps the silent item).
- **Tightened**: S4 now asserts the chain's dependent is picked within 5 minutes of its upstream closing — the assertion that would have been red before the F1 poke existed.

The see-it-fail evidence ran in the natural direction: the [coverage drift-guard](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/tasks-dispatch-design-analysis-mxj7x6/docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/coverage.test.mjs) went red mid-change (citing the deleted S9b, then missing §15.14–21 rows) and forced the README map to catch up, and S4's new assertion passes only with the close-time drain in the sim. Final state: 42/42 sim tests, 1768/1768 across the tracked suite.

One honest caveat, already tracked: these tests pin the **simulator**, i.e. the design's specified behavior — the engine in `engine/scheduler/queue/` doesn't implement heartbeat/poke/decoupling yet, and its own `engine-tests/scheduler/queue/` tests will grow with that work in [#883](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/883).

Honest audit: **no, not enough — and your question exposes a real fidelity gap I papered over with a "prose" coverage row.** Three specific holes in the sim as merged:

1. **No run granularity.** The sim's `executorRun` is an instantaneous loop (hardcoded cap of 10, not even the engine's `maxItems = 3`), and no test asserts how many items one run completes. Worse, it *starts* all picked items' work phases concurrently in the same virtual instant — but the real engine's run is **serial**: it awaits each item's work step before the next pick. Serial occupancy is the very thing the work-as-work review priced (F21), and the sim doesn't model it — I marked §15.17 "prose", which your question correctly reads as "not tested".
2. **No per-run completion assertion.** Multi-task scenarios exist (S4 drains four items, S18 fans out), but nothing asserts per-run item counts.
3. **The next-run trigger is only half modeled.** Tick drains, label events, and my new close-time drain are simulated; **self-re-dispatch** (the design's answer for a run that exits with items left) is not — leftover items silently wait for the tick, and no test names which trigger picked which item.

I'll fix all three: model executor runs as serial timed objects with `maxItems` and a recorded trigger (`tick-drain` / `label-event` / `close-drain` / `re-dispatch`), add self-re-dispatch, and add scenarios asserting per-run counts and the trigger chain. ### S34/S35 — run granularity, and what causes the next run (F23)

The first simulator brought up to this review still modeled the executor as an
instantaneous loop: all picked items' work phases started in the same virtual
instant, nothing bounded a run, and no test could say *which run* did *what* —
exactly the shape F21 warned about, reproduced in the model meant to catch it
(owner question, 2026-08-15: *"asserted that each executor run completes just
one task from the queue? Have you simulated what causes the next executor
run?"*). The sim now models runs as first-class objects: **serial** (the next
pick waits for the previous item to settle — roll, close, hand-off, or
failure), **bounded** (`maxItems`, default one, per the owner's ruling), and
**caused** (every run records its trigger: `tick-drain` — the cron workflow's
own drain job, started by the job graph, no event involved; `label-event` — a
foreign token's `task:ready`/`task:urgent`; `close-drain` — the converge path,
when its readiness re-check leaves something pickable; `re-dispatch` — a full
run chaining a fresh one via `workflow_dispatch`, which the default
`GITHUB_TOKEN` may fire). A run whose runner dies records no end and settles
nothing — the leash is its recovery, unchanged.

- **S34** (maxItems 1, two tasks with real work plus the day's rolls): every
  completed run settled **at most one item**, the working runs exactly one;
  both work items converged well inside the hour, so the record must show —
  and does — `tick-drain` first, then `re-dispatch`/`close-drain` chaining
  the queue dry with no second cron fire involved.
- **S35** (maxItems 3, two 30-minute tasks): one run took both items and its
  work steps **serialized** — the second evaluation lands only after the
  first item's close, a full work bound apart — pinning the occupancy model
  §10 prices (executor work serializes; agent work does not).
