+## I. The work-as-work review (owner corrections, 2026-08-15)
+
+Two owner rulings landed the same day, and this section replays what they
+touch. First the **invocation reversal** (recorded in DESIGN §6.6/§7/§15.11
+when the mechanism was built): the routine-fire endpoint has no idempotency
+key, and the owner's correction was *don't create the duplicates* — one call
+per item, never retried, so at-least-once invocation, the hand-off retry (F3)
+and the agent-side claim lease (F5) all delete. Then the **work-as-work
+correction**: *"The pre work is not pre work. It's work. Sometimes there's
+also agentic work. The work can take time. The work can crash. The work
+creates PRs. The work is a lot."* The executor-side work step is the whole
+task for most of the fleet; every sizing assumption built on "the drain is
+quick" was re-derived. The simulator was brought up to both in this same
+change — the sections below supersede S9/S10/S31 as previously written.
+
+### S9/S10, replayed under at-most-once invocation
+
+- **S9a (refused)**: the endpoint answers with an error — a token, URL or
+  routine is wrong, which no retry fixes. The item converges `needs-human` at
+  once, naming the cause; zero sessions exist. (Replaces the bounded
+  revert-and-retry of F3, which assumed retrying was safe.)
+- **S10a (unanswered, session started)**: the call times out client-side but
+  did create a session. Nothing retries — so exactly one session exists, and
+  it converges the item itself. The duplicate-session problem F5's lease
+  solved can no longer occur.
+- **S10b (unanswered, no session)**: the call created nothing. The item stays
+  `task:agent` wearing the outcome-unknown comment, silent, until the
+  janitor's agent leash brings it to triage within hours. The cost of never
+  guessing is bounded latency on a rare platform failure — the trade the
+  owner chose over any path that could put two sessions on one item.
+
+### S31, replayed under the heartbeat (F20 — the leash inflation)
+
+F17 as first written made the executing leash exceed every task's work bound —
+which, once the work step is priced as the work, inflates the leash to the
+heaviest task in the fleet and slows every dead-executor recovery to match.
+The heartbeat replaces that arithmetic:
+
+- **S31**: the wiring check shrinks to the one relation the heartbeat needs —
+  interval well inside the leash; a violating configuration is refused at
+  construction.
+- **S31b**: with heartbeats switched off, the original livelock is still
+  demonstrable — a silent long work step is reclaimed alive every cycle,
+  re-executes forever, never converges. This is why the heartbeat is
+  contract, not courtesy.
+- **S31c**: a 130-minute work step heartbeats through two leash windows, is
+  never reclaimed, and converges once — long work is now legal.
+- **S31d**: the runner dies 40 minutes into that work; heartbeats stop, and
+  the reclaim lands within ~leash of the last heartbeat — recovery is bounded
+  by the leash, never by the work's duration. The re-pick converges (the work
+  step's re-entrancy contract, F12, unchanged).
+
+### S33 — the readiness re-check at close (F1, reopened)
+
+Two fan-out members converge; the close of the second readies the fan-in **in
+code, within the minute**, and the follow-on drain runs it — no tick in the
+path (`ready` carries `by: close`). S4 gains the matching assertion on the
+yield side: the chain's dependent is picked within minutes of its upstream
+closing. A close by hand still runs no engine code; S18 keeps the tick as
+that path's backstop, unchanged.
+
+### S34/S35 — run granularity, and what causes the next run (F23)
+
+The first simulator brought up to this review still modeled the executor as an
+instantaneous loop: all picked items' work phases started in the same virtual
+instant, nothing bounded a run, and no test could say *which run* did *what* —
+exactly the shape F21 warned about, reproduced in the model meant to catch it
+(owner question, 2026-08-15: *"asserted that each executor run completes just
+one task from the queue? Have you simulated what causes the next executor
+run?"*). The sim now models runs as first-class objects: **serial** (the next
+pick waits for the previous item to settle — roll, close, hand-off, or
+failure), **bounded** (`maxItems`, default one, per the owner's ruling), and
+**caused** (every run records its trigger: `tick-drain` — the cron workflow's
+own drain job, started by the job graph, no event involved; `label-event` — a
+foreign token's `task:ready`/`task:urgent`; `close-drain` — the converge path,
+when its readiness re-check leaves something pickable; `re-dispatch` — a full
+run chaining a fresh one via `workflow_dispatch`, which the default
+`GITHUB_TOKEN` may fire). A run whose runner dies records no end and settles
+nothing — the leash is its recovery, unchanged.

+  first item's close, a full work bound apart — pinning the occupancy model

Done — pushed to [PR #884](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/884). Answers to everything you asked this turn:

**Were there enough multi-task / one-item-per-run tests?** No — your question caught a real sim fidelity bug, now logged as **F23** in the [findings ledger](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/tasks-dispatch-design-analysis-mxj7x6/docs/tasks-dispatch/SCENARIOS.md): the executor was modeled as an instantaneous unbounded loop that started all picked items' work *concurrently* — no `maxItems`, no run boundaries, no occupancy. Fixed in [sim.mjs](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/tasks-dispatch-design-analysis-mxj7x6/docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/sim.mjs): runs are now first-class — **serial** (next pick only after the previous item settles: roll, close, hand-off, or failure), **bounded** (`maxItems`, default **one** per your ruling), and **caused** (every run records its trigger). New tests: **S34** asserts every completed run settles at most one item (working runs exactly one) and that a busy morning drains with no second cron fire; **S35** asserts that a multi-item run (maxItems 3) serializes its work steps — the second evaluation lands a full work bound after the first, pinning the occupancy model. A run whose runner dies records no end and settles nothing — the leash recovers it, as before.

**What causes the next executor run?** Now an enumerable, asserted list (DESIGN §10, S34): (1) **tick-drain** — the cron workflow's own drain job via the job graph (`needs: tick`), no event involved; this is also the answer to "how does the first executor after the tick work"; (2) **label-event** — a foreign token's `task:ready`/`task:urgent` (own-token label writes fire nothing); (3) **close-drain** — the converging side triggers a drain when its readiness re-check leaves something pickable; (4) **re-dispatch** — a run that hits `maxItems` with items left starts a fresh run.

**Can one Action invoke another?** Yes — `POST .../actions/workflows/{file}/dispatches` against a workflow declaring `on: workflow_dispatch`, with `actions: write`. The load-bearing platform fact: the `GITHUB_TOKEN` recursion guard **exempts** `workflow_dispatch` (and `repository_dispatch`), so the tick can explicitly start the executor and an executor can start another executor on the default token — both target workflows are already wired (`on: workflow_dispatch`, `actions: write`). Caveats: the API's 204 means *queued*, not started, and `workflow_call` is a different thing (composition inside one run).

Verification: sim 44/44, full tracked suite 1770/1770. Engine follow-ups noted on [#883](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/883) (`DEFAULT_MAX_ITEMS` 3→1, dispatch plumbing).

- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.

- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

Here's the exact trace for two fresh items A and B under the current design (`maxItems` = 1), with each cause named:

**Tick, :17.** The tick job creates/readies items A and B. These label writes use the workflow's own `GITHUB_TOKEN`, so they emit **no events** — nothing is triggered *by the labeling itself*.

**Executor run 1 — cause: the job graph.** The drain job runs because it's the second job of the same cron workflow (`drain: needs: tick`) — a structural dependency, not an event. It lists `task:ready`, picks A (oldest), claims it, evaluates, does the work, converges A. That's one settled item = `maxItems`, so the run ends. At run end it re-reads the queue: **B is still pickable → it fires `workflow_dispatch` on the executor workflow** (the `GITHUB_TOKEN` is explicitly allowed to fire that event type). This is the re-dispatch.

**Executor run 2 — cause: run 1's re-dispatch.** The dispatched run picks B, works it, converges B. One settled item = `maxItems`, run ends, re-reads the queue: **nothing pickable → no dispatch.** Separately, B's close ran the readiness re-check (F1) — nothing became ready, nothing pickable → no close-drain either.

**Why no third run: every trigger is conditional on live queue state, read at the moment of triggering.** The re-dispatch fires only when the ending run sees items still pickable; the close-drain fires only when a close leaves something pickable; there is no unconditional "always chain another run" anywhere. So with the queue empty, both conditions read false and the chain simply stops.

One honesty note, because your trace has a wrinkle in it: when run 1 closes A, **two** causes actually point at B — A's close-drain (B was pickable at that moment) *and* run 1's end-of-run re-dispatch. Both may fire. That's deliberate, not a bug: the triggers are designed as overlapping, at-least-once delivery (this is the same posture that makes lost label events harmless), and **deduplication happens at the pick and the claim, never at the trigger**. Whichever run arrives first claims B; the other lists `task:ready`, finds nothing it can take, and exits quietly — a recorded run that settled zero items. The invariant the design maintains is therefore *zero extra work* (the lease guarantees one execution per item), not *zero extra runs* — a redundant no-op run costs a runner spin-up and nothing else, and the same-instant tick an hour later behaves identically: pick empty, exit quiet. This is exactly what S34 asserts: per-run settled counts never exceed one, both items converge within the hour, and the run log shows `tick-drain` then `re-dispatch`/`close-drain` — with any surplus runs ending `settled: 0`.

If you'd rather the close-drain *not* fire when the closing run will re-dispatch anyway (one trigger per hand-over instead of overlapping ones), that's a design tweak I can fold in — say the word.

Three corrections taken, one question to answer, and one decision that's yours:

1. **`maxItems` dies.** You're right — one item isn't a configuration value, it's what an executor run *is*. I'll remove the knob from the design and the sim entirely (and note on #883 that the engine's `DEFAULT_MAX_ITEMS`/`CLAUDINITE_MAX_ITEMS` surface goes too). S35 ("serial within a multi-item run") becomes meaningless and gets deleted — serial occupancy across items is simply the re-dispatch chain.
2. **Randomized pick, now.** Your rebuttal lands: the stale-ready escalation cares about ~2-period hangs, and random pick reorders items by *minutes* — my FIFO-aging objection was weighing something the janitor never looks at. I'll adopt randomize-after-urgent immediately (reversing decision 20's "with width"), with a seeded PRNG in the sim so tests stay deterministic.
3. **The broken train, traced honestly.** 5 ready items, run 2 dies mid-work (crash, kill, timeout — same thing): its item stays `task:executing`, and **the re-dispatch never fires, because it fires at run *end*** — the train stalls. As designed today, what restarts it is the **next hourly tick's drain job**: the other 3 ready items just get picked (up to ~1h late), and the dead item rejoins after the leash reclaims it (~1h of heartbeat silence, then the tick after that). **Is there a sim test? No** — S8/S31d test the dead *item's* recovery, but nothing asserts the *rest of the queue* survives a dead run. I'll add S36 either way.
4. **Is there a GitHub Actions mechanism that helps? Yes, a clean one**: a continuation job in the executor workflow — `needs: execute` with `if: failure() || cancelled()` — which GitHub runs on a *fresh runner* even when the execute job timed out, was cancelled, or its runner was lost. Its only step re-dispatches the executor workflow, so the train resumes in ~a minute instead of ~an hour. It can't double-work anything: the dead item still wears `task:executing` (untouched until the leash), and the fresh run just picks the next ready item under the ordinary lease. The tick stays the backstop for the case where the whole workflow run is lost.

1	# The dispatch simulator — SCENARIOS.md, executable
2	
3	A discrete-event simulator of the [tasks-dispatch DESIGN](../DESIGN.md), so
4	the scenario play-throughs in [SCENARIOS.md](../SCENARIOS.md) run as tests
5	instead of living only as prose. Owner request, 2026-08-13: *"add the 'at
6	time x — y happens' to the tests, and then execute the simulator — this will
7	help us make the design more robust."* It has caught two real spec bugs prose
8	replay missed — **F13** (the occurrence guard's missing closed-at half) and
9	**F14** (the stale rule can never see a stuck *blocked* item) — which is the
10	whole argument for its existence.
11	
12	- [`sim.mjs`](sim.mjs) — the model: a virtual clock and an ordered event
13	  queue (no threads, no waits, no wall clock), an in-memory issue store, and
14	  the mechanism as DESIGN.md specifies it — the tick's three jobs, the
15	  executor's pick/claim/evaluate/roll with the verified lease, prework →
16	  hand-off → converge as timed phases, the invocation layer (bounded retry,
17	  at-least-once duplicates, the agent-side lease), the janitor's three
18	  rules, and the force/re-queue levers. `afterMode: 'blocked-by'` exists
19	  solely so S24 can demonstrate the starvation that ruled that wiring out.
20	- [`scenarios.test.mjs`](scenarios.test.mjs) — the play-throughs, numbered
21	  to match SCENARIOS.md. Each test schedules world events at instants
22	  (`sim.at('2026-08-12T09:03Z', …)`), runs the clock across a window, and
23	  asserts on the issue store and event log. Multi-executor contention runs
24	  through `sim.raceExecutorsAt(…)`, which gives two executors the same stale
25	  snapshot and lets the lease sort it out.

You were right about the janitor — the stale-ready escalation fires at ~2 *periods*, so minute-scale reordering was never something it could see; my FIFO-aging objection was weightless. The sim uses a seeded PRNG (`pickSeed`) so every scenario replays identically, and the whole 44-test suite now runs under the shuffle.

**The broken train — 5 items, run 2 dies/times out, what starts run 3?** As previously designed: nothing until the next hourly tick, because the re-dispatch fires at run *end* and a dead run never gets there — an honest gap. Now fixed with the GitHub Actions mechanism you asked about: the executor workflow gains a **failure-continuation job** — `needs: execute` with `if: failure() || cancelled()` — which the platform runs on a **fresh runner** even when the execute job timed out, was cancelled, or lost its runner entirely. Its single step re-dispatches the workflow (`workflow_dispatch`, which `GITHUB_TOKEN` may fire). So: the remaining 3 ready items resume within ~a minute; the dead run's own item — still wearing `task:executing` — is untouchable until the leash reclaims it from its last heartbeat (~1h), then rejoins; and the hourly tick drain remains the backstop for the pathological case where the whole workflow run vanishes, continuation included. **And yes, there is now a sim test**: [S36](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/tasks-dispatch-design-analysis-mxj7x6/docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/scenarios.test.mjs) runs exactly your scenario — five tasks with work, the run executing one dies two minutes in — and asserts the four unaffected items drain within minutes with a `failure-redispatch`-triggered run on the record, the crashed item converges only after the leash reclaim, and no run ever settles more than its one item. §10's run-cause list grows to five, §11's recovery table gains the dead-run row.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

Comment class: feature | other
Your intent split is right, and the design should say it explicitly:

- **Cancelling one executor run is intent 1** ("this run is stalled, let the system move on") — and that's already exactly how the mechanism treats it: cancellation is indistinguishable from a crash, the continuation job keeps the train moving, and the cancelled run's item is freed by the leash (~1h) rather than immediately. Cancelling runs one at a time can never achieve intent 2, because the hourly tick and events keep spawning runs — which is why intent 2 deserves its own lever.
- **Intent 2 gets `CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL`**, as you propose: every Claudinite workflow (scheduler and executor) checks it as its first act and exits cleanly, firing nothing. One nuance worth stating: an *in-flight* continuation job may still fire one re-dispatch, but that fresh run sees the variable and parks — so the train stops one hop after suspension, at the latest. In-flight agent sessions aren't workflows and finish on their own (suspension gates *starts*, not running work). Items freeze in place with no labels touched, which is what makes suspend/resume stateless. Implementation note: the natural carrier is a **repo Actions variable** (`vars.CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL` stamped into workflow env) — settable in the UI or via API with no commit, unlike the existing `dormant` config which is a declared standing state requiring a commit; the two are different tools and I'll state the distinction.
- **Resume**: clear the variable, and then — *almost* what you said, with one correction: the lever is manually running the **scheduler** workflow, not the bare executor. The tick's jobs are the recovery half (reclaim the claims of runs killed during the stoppage, ready due items) and its drain then picks up; a bare executor run would drain ready items but skip the reclaim/ready half. Doing nothing also works: the next cron tick (≤1h) performs the identical self-heal.

Implementing sim-first with tests for both scenarios:

input.old_string:
- **`manual` tasks** are simply tasks the tick never instantiates: their items
  are only ever created by hand or by other tasks. The frequency token
  survives; the special-case slot resolution for it dies.
input.new_string:
- **Cancelling one executor run means "move on", and the mechanism already
  reads it that way** (owner, 2026-08-16). A single cancellation is
  indistinguishable from a crash: the failure continuation (§10) keeps the
  train moving, and the cancelled run's item is freed by the leash. What a
  single cancellation can *never* mean is "stop the system" — the tick and
  events keep spawning runs — so that intent gets its own lever:
- **Suspending the whole queue is `CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL`** (owner,
  2026-08-16): a repo Actions **variable** (`vars.*`, stamped into each
  workflow's env by the wiring — settable in the UI or over the API, **no
  commit**), which every Claudinite workflow — tick and executor alike —
  checks as its *first act* and, when true, exits cleanly having fired
  nothing. The train parks at most one hop after suspension (an already
  in-flight continuation may fire one re-dispatch; that fresh run sees the
  variable and parks). Suspension gates workflow *starts* only: in-flight
  runs and agent sessions finish on their own — cancel those by hand if the
  hold is urgent — and items freeze exactly where they are, no labels
  touched, which is what makes the hold stateless. This is not dormancy:

2

4	[DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) specifies it (owner request on #784: *"play them out
5	using this mechanism, and see if there are conceptual issues we missed"*).
6	Each scenario ends in a verdict: **holds** (the design handles it as written),
7	or a numbered **finding**. The findings ledger at the end classifies every
8	finding and says what was done about it — some amended DESIGN.md in this same
9	change, some are owner calls added to its §15.
10	
11	> **Read §H, then §I, for the current mechanism.** Sections A–G record rounds
12	> one and two (the tick-evaluates models); the owner's **standing-item model**
13	> (2026-08-13) replaced generation, and §H replays everything it touches. §I
14	> records the **work-as-work review** (2026-08-15) — the correction that the
15	> work step IS the work — and the invocation reversal (at-most-once, the
16	> agent lease deleted) decided the same day: where earlier sections conflict
17	> with §I, §I is the design as it stands. The superseded sections are kept
18	> because their reasoning is the record.
19	>
20	> **The scenarios are executable.** [`sim/`](sim/) holds a discrete-event
21	> simulator of the mechanism (virtual clock, no threads, no waits) and
22	> [`sim/scenarios.test.mjs`](sim/scenarios.test.mjs) plays the §H scenarios
23	> against it as `at time X, Y happens` tests, run by CI. A future design
24	> change should change the simulator first and let the red tests name the
25	> scenarios it breaks. Its first run caught F13 — a double-execution bug

One more decision to implement (2026-08-15/16 review, DESIGN §15.24): **the operator hold**.

- [ ] Every Claudinite workflow (scheduler + executor) stamps `CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL: ${{ vars.CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL }}` into its env and the engine entry points (`tick.mjs`, `executor.mjs`) exit cleanly as their **first act** when it is true — before any read, like the dormancy gate — firing no dispatch. While off: the only full-stop lever is dormancy, which needs a commit.
- [ ] The failure-continuation job's re-dispatch step needs no special casing: the fresh run it starts checks the variable and parks — but verify the continuation job itself doesn't loop on a suspended run (it fires only from a *failed/cancelled* execute job; a suspended run exits 0, so no loop).
- [ ] Resume needs no code: clearing the variable + the next cron tick self-heals (reclaim, ready, drain). Document in the workflow header that the impatient path is dispatching the **scheduler** workflow, not the bare executor.

Sim reference: `S37` (freeze semantics — no pick after the hold, in-flight work finishes, items frozen ready) and `S38` (cancel + suspend + resume, recovered by the next tick unaided).

Landed and pushed to [PR #884](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/884). The answers, as now written into the design:

**Cancellation intent** — you're right that it's the first, and the design now says so explicitly ([DESIGN §8](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/tasks-dispatch-design-analysis-mxj7x6/docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md)): cancelling one run means "this run is stalled, move on," and the mechanism already serves it — cancellation is indistinguishable from a crash, the failure continuation keeps the train moving, the leash frees the item. The second intent can't be expressed by cancelling runs at all (the tick and events keep spawning them), so it gets your lever.

**`CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL`** — adopted as designed, with one implementation note: the carrier is a repo Actions **variable** (`vars.*`, stamped into each workflow's env), since that's settable in the UI or over the API with **no commit** — unlike the existing `dormant` config, which is the declared-standing-state tool. Every workflow checks it as its first act and exits having fired nothing. Two boundary facts stated honestly: an in-flight continuation may fire one re-dispatch, but that fresh run parks at its first act — so the train stops one hop after suspension at most; and suspension gates workflow *starts* only — in-flight runs and agent sessions finish on their own, and items freeze exactly where they are with no labels touched, which is what makes the hold stateless.

**Resume** — clearing the variable is the whole action, with one correction to your suggestion: the impatient lever is a hand-dispatched **scheduler** run (tick + drain), not the bare executor — the tick's reclaim/ready jobs are the half that recovers claims killed during the hold and wakes what came due, and a bare executor run would skip them. Doing nothing also works: the next cron tick (≤1h) performs the identical self-heal unaided.

**Sim tests, both scenarios** ([scenarios.test.mjs](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/tasks-dispatch-design-analysis-mxj7x6/docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/scenarios.test.mjs)): **S37** — five tasks mid-drain, hold set at 04:30: zero picks or evaluations after the hold, the in-flight run finishes its item (gates-starts-not-work, asserted precisely), the in-flight continuation's re-dispatch parks as a recorded `suspended-skip`, every later cron fire exits at start, and every never-picked item freezes as `task:ready`. **S38** — your combined case: user cancels a stalled run mid-work *and* suspends before the continuation lands (intent 2 overriding intent 1's train), then hours later just clears the variable — the next cron tick alone reclaims the cancelled run's long-silent claim and drains the queue to full convergence, proving resume needs no dedicated mechanism. One assertion of mine was initially wrong and the sim right: I first asserted "no closes after the hold," which the in-flight run legitimately violates — the invariant is "no new picks."

Verification: sim 46/46, full tracked suite 1772/1772. Engine wiring checkboxed on [#883](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/883), including the note that the continuation job can't loop on a suspended run (it fires only from failed/cancelled jobs; a suspended run exits 0).

> ✅ All done — DESIGN §8/§15.24, SCENARIOS §I S37/S38, sim + tests, all on PR [#884](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/884); "LGTM" merges it. Open: engine implementation ([#883](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/883)), tick rename ([#877](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/877)).
